All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must give a single exact real number equal to the infimum of all c in [0,1] for which the stated finite triangle-free homomorphism target exists, with a proof that this is the infimum. It need not determine whether the property holds at the infimum itself.

One agent, working alone, was asked to find the answer, which it was not told, and to prove it, writing Python that checks every step. Its run ended: all agents idle, the judge found the proof complete. Read from its record, the answer it ended with is \frac{1}{9}. It may be wrong, and it may not have proved it: agents sometimes stop at bounds or partial results, and sometimes claim a proof of a wrong answer anyway. Below, "the team" is this one agent: it had no partners, no Slack channel and no shared workspace. 7	I will prove both statements needed for this conclusion:
8	
9	* for every \(c>1/9\), there is a bounded triangle-free homomorphic target;
10	* for every \(c<1/9\), no such target exists.
11	
12	The distinction between forbidding triangles in the **target** and forbidding both triangles and pentagons in the target is important here.
13	
14	## 1. Turning the problem into a colouring problem
15	
16	For a triangle-free graph \(G\), define \(J(G)\) on \(V(G)\) by
17	\[
18	xy\in E(J(G))
19	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
20	\text{there is a walk of length \(3\) from \(x\) to \(y\) in \(G\)}.
21	\]
22	There are no loops: a closed walk of length \(3\) would give a triangle. Also, \(G\subseteq J(G)\), using the walk \(x,y,x,y\).
23	
24	We need two observations.
25	
26	**Observation 1.** If \(G\to H\), where \(H\) is triangle-free, then
27	\[
28	\chi(J(G))\le |V(H)|.
29	\]
30	Indeed, the endpoints of a length-\(3\) walk cannot have the same image: that would give a closed length-\(3\) walk in \(H\).
31	
32	**Observation 2.** For each \(q\), there is a finite triangle-free graph \(U_q\) such that
33	\[
34	\chi(J(G))\le q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\to U_q.
35	\]
36	
37	Here is an explicit choice. Its vertices are
38	\[
39	(i,S),\qquad i\in[q],\quad S\subseteq[q]\setminus\{i\},
40	\]
41	with
42	\[
43	(i,S)(j,T)\in E(U_q)
44	\iff i\in T,\ j\in S,\ S\cap T=\varnothing.
45	\]
46	This graph is triangle-free: in a triangle with first coordinates \(i,j,k\), the number \(k\) would belong to both sets attached to the first two vertices.
47	
48	Given a proper colouring \(\kappa\) of \(J(G)\), map
49	\[
50	v\longmapsto
51	\left(\kappa(v),\{\kappa(w):w\in N_G(v)\}\right).
52	\]
53	For an edge \(uv\), the two neighbourhood-colour sets are disjoint: a common colour would occur at the endpoints of a walk \(x,u,v,y\). Thus this is a homomorphism to \(U_q\).
54	
55	Consequently, the upper-bound problem is exactly that of bounding \(\chi(J(G))\).
56	
57	We will also use:
58	\[
59	xy\in E(J(G))\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_G(x)\cap N_G(y)=\varnothing
60	\tag{1}
61	\]
62	when \(G\) has no \(C_3,C_5\). Otherwise there is a closed odd walk of length \(5\), which contains a \(C_3\) or a \(C_5\).
63	
64	---
65	
66	# 2. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
67	
68	Fix \(c>1/9\). Put
69	\[
70	\rho=\min\left\{\frac{9c-1}{30},\frac1{100}\right\},
71	\qquad
72	\beta=c-2\rho,\qquad \gamma=c-\rho.
73	\]
74	Then
75	\[
76	\beta>0,\qquad 6\beta+3\gamma=9c-15\rho>1.
77	\tag{2}
78	\]
79	
80	We first construct a bounded partition suitable for arbitrary vertices, including exceptional vertices.
81	
82	## 2.1 A weighted regularity partition
83	
84	For disjoint nonempty sets \(A,B\), write
85	\[
86	d(A,B)=\frac{e(A,B)}{|A||B|}.
87	\]
88	A pair is \(\varepsilon\)-regular if all \(X\subseteq A,Y\subseteq B\) with
89	\[
90	|X|\ge\varepsilon|A|,\qquad |Y|\ge\varepsilon|B|
91	\]
92	satisfy \(|d(X,Y)-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon\).
93	
94	Choose
95	\[
96	\alpha=\rho,\qquad d=\eta=\frac{\rho}{10},
97	\qquad \varepsilon=\left(\frac{\rho}{100}\right)^2.
98	\]
99	
100	For all sufficiently large \(n\), every \(n\)-vertex graph of minimum degree at least \(cn\) has a partition
101	\[
102	V(G)=V_0\sqcup V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k
103	\]
104	and a graph \(R\) on \([k]\), where \(k\) is bounded in terms of \(c\), such that:
105	
106	1. \(|V_0|\le\rho n\);
107	2. every \(V_i\), \(i\ge1\), has size at least a positive constant times \(n\);
108	3. every edge \(ij\in E(R)\) represents an \(\varepsilon\)-regular pair of density at least \(d\);
109	4. writing \(w(I)=\sum_{i\in I}|V_i|\),
110	   \[
111	   w(N_R(i))\ge\gamma n\qquad(i\in[k]).
112	   \tag{3}
113	   \]
114	
115	Here is the regularity argument, included to specify precisely what is used.
116	
117	Start with a bounded partition whose parts have size at most \(\eta n\). For a partition \(\mathcal P\), use the energy
118	\[
119	\mathcal E(\mathcal P)
120	=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{A,B\in\mathcal P}|A||B|d(A,B)^2,
121	\]
122	including diagonal terms, with adjacency-matrix density on \(A\times A\). It lies in \([0,1]\) and does not decrease under refinement, by convexity.
123	
124	For every irregular pair choose witnessing subsets and refine all parts by all witnesses. An irregular ordered pair \(A,B\) increases energy by more than
125	\[
126	\varepsilon^4\frac{|A||B|}{n^2}.
127	\]
128	Thus, while the total weight of irregular ordered pairs exceeds \(\varepsilon n^2\), energy increases by more than \(\varepsilon^5\). This process stops after at most \(\lceil\varepsilon^{-5}\rceil\) refinements. A partition with \(k\) parts is refined into at most \(k2^k\) parts, so the final number of parts has a bound \(M=M(c)\).
129	
130	Delete every part having irregular partners of total size greater than \(\sqrt\varepsilon n\). Their total size is at most \(\sqrt\varepsilon n\). Also delete parts smaller than \(\eta n/M\); their total size is at most \(\eta n\). These deleted vertices form \(V_0\).
131	
132	Join retained parts in \(R\) when their pair is regular and has density at least \(d\). For a retained part \(V_i\), average the degrees of its vertices. Contributions from deleted vertices, its own part, irregular partners and low-density regular partners are at most
133	\[
134	(\eta+\sqrt\varepsilon)n+\eta n+\sqrt\varepsilon n+dn.
135	\]
136	Therefore
137	\[
138	w(N_R(i))
139	\ge\bigl(c-2\eta-2\sqrt\varepsilon-d\bigr)n
140	\ge(c-\rho)n.
141	\]
142	Also \(\eta+\sqrt\varepsilon<\rho\). This proves all the asserted partition properties.
143	
144	## 2.2 Supports and two consequences of having no \(C_3,C_5\)
145	
146	For **every** vertex \(v\), including \(v\in V_0\), define its support
147	\[
148	S(v)=
149	\left\{i\in[k]:|N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge\alpha |V_i|\right\}.
150	\]
151	The number of neighbours outside the union of its support parts is at most
152	\[
153	|V_0|+\alpha n\le2\rho n.
154	\]
155	Hence
156	\[
157	\left|N_G(v)\cap\bigcup_{i\in S(v)}V_i\right|\ge\beta n.
158	\tag{4}
159	\]
160	
161	For sufficiently large \(n\), regularity gives the following two facts.
162	
163	**Fact A.** If \(xy\in E(G)\), then
164	\[
165	N_R(S(x))\cap N_R(S(y))=\varnothing.
166	\tag{5}
167	\]
168	
169	Indeed, if a cluster \(C\) is adjacent in \(R\) to \(A\in S(x)\) and \(B\in S(y)\), regularity supplies a path
170	\[
171	x-a-z-b-y
172	\]
173	with \(a\in A,z\in C,b\in B\), all five vertices distinct. Together with \(xy\), this is a pentagon. This works also when \(A=B\): almost every vertex of \(C\) has many neighbours in each of the two prescribed positive-sized subsets of \(A\).
174	
175	**Fact B.** If \(x=y\), or if \(x,y\) have a common neighbour, then there is no edge of \(R\) between \(S(x)\) and \(S(y)\).
176	
177	For \(x=y\), such an edge gives a triangle through \(x\). If \(x,y\) have common neighbour \(z\), it supplies a path
178	\[
179	x-a-b-y,
180	\]
181	which together with \(y-z-x\) gives a pentagon.
182	
183	These applications of regularity need no induced-cycle assumption. To make the distinctness details explicit, remove the at most three already prescribed vertices from the relevant neighbourhood subsets. Their remaining relative sizes are at least \(\alpha/2>\varepsilon\) once the parts are large enough. Regularity then supplies the required edge or two-edge path, since \(\varepsilon<d/4\). For example, part size at least \(100/(\alpha d)\) is more than sufficient.
184	
185	## 2.3 Small supports are easy to colour
186	
187	Call a support **small** if
188	\[
189	w(S)<2\beta n.
190	\]
191	Let \(W\) be the vertices having small support.
192	
193	Each fixed-support class in \(W\) is independent in \(J(G)\). Indeed, by (4), any two vertices in it have at least \(\beta n\) neighbours in a set of size less than \(2\beta n\), so their neighbourhoods intersect. Apply (1).
194	
195	Thus \(J(G)[W]\) has a proper colouring \(\kappa_W\) with at most
196	\[
197	p=2^k
198	\]
199	colours, by using the support itself as the colour.
200	
201	For each vertex \(v\), record the following three pieces of information:
202	\[
203	\begin{aligned}
204	S(v),\qquad
205	L(v)&=\{\kappa_W(w):w\in N_G(v)\cap W\},\\
206	T(v)&=\{S(w):w\in N_G(v)\}.
207	\end{aligned}
208	\tag{6}
209	\]
210	There are at most
211	\[
212	p\,2^p\,2^p=p\,2^{2p}
213	\tag{7}
214	\]
215	possible records.
216	
217	I claim that these records properly colour \(J(G)\).
218	
219	## 2.4 The nine-part counting argument
220	
221	Suppose otherwise. Let \(u,v\) have the same record, with a walk
222	\[
223	u-a-b-v
224	\tag{8}
225	\]
226	of length \(3\).
227	
228	The endpoints cannot belong to \(W\), by the preceding fixed-support colouring.
229	
230	Nor can \(a\in W\). If it did, \(L(u)=L(v)\) would give \(a'\in N(v)\cap W\) with
231	\(\kappa_W(a')=\kappa_W(a)\). But \(a,b,v,a'\) is a length-\(3\) walk, contradicting properness of \(\kappa_W\). The case \(b\in W\) is symmetric.
232	
233	Put
234	\[
235	P=S(u)=S(v),\qquad Q=S(a),\qquad D=S(b).
236	\]
237	All three are non-small, so
238	\[
239	w(P),w(Q),w(D)\ge2\beta n.
240	\tag{9}
241	\]
242	
243	By Fact A, applied to the three edges of (8), the sets
244	\[
245	N_R(P),\quad N_R(Q),\quad N_R(D)
246	\]
247	are pairwise disjoint. Since every vertex of \(R\) has a neighbour by (3), this also implies that \(P,Q,D\) are pairwise disjoint.
248	
249	Next, \(P\cup Q\cup D\) is independent in \(R\):
250	
251	* each individual support is independent, by Fact B with \(x=y\);
252	* there are no edges between \(P,Q\), since \(a,v\) share neighbour \(b\);
253	* there are no edges between \(P,D\), since \(u,b\) share neighbour \(a\);
254	* because \(T(u)=T(v)\), some \(b'\in N(u)\) has \(S(b')=D\). The vertices \(a,b'\) share neighbour \(u\), so Fact B rules out edges between \(Q,D\).
255	
256	Consequently, these **six sets of clusters** are pairwise disjoint:
257	\[
258	P,\ Q,\ D,\ N_R(P),\ N_R(Q),\ N_R(D).
259	\]
260	Each of the last three has weight at least \(\gamma n\), by (3), and each of the first three has weight at least \(2\beta n\). Therefore
261	\[
262	n\ge6\beta n+3\gamma n>n,
263	\]
264	by (2), a contradiction.
265	
266	Thus (6) is a proper bounded colouring of \(J(G)\).
267	
268	For all sufficiently large \(n\), (7) bounds \(\chi(J(G))\) solely in terms of \(c\). Enlarge that bound to cover smaller graphs as well, using at most \(n\) colours for an \(n\)-vertex graph. Observation 2 then gives one finite triangle-free target \(U_q\) for every graph in question.
269	
270	This proves the upper half.
271

274	# 3. Lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails
275	
276	We use Kneser graphs
277	\[
278	F=KG(m,k),
279	\]
280	whose vertices are the \(k\)-subsets of \([m]\), with disjoint sets adjacent. Their chromatic number is
281	\[
282	\chi(KG(m,k))=m-2k+2.
283	\tag{10}
284	\]
285	Only the lower bound in (10) is needed. A proof is included in Section 4.
286	
287	Fix a proposed triangle-free target \(H\), with \(h\) vertices. We may assume \(h\ge2\), since \(K_2\) already rules out targets with fewer vertices.
288	
289	Choose
290	\[
291	m=2k+h-1.
292	\]
293	Then \(\chi(F)\ge h+1\).
294	
295	## 3.1 The sparse core
296	
297	Orient each edge \(ST\) of \(F\) arbitrarily and replace it by
298	\[
299	S-a_{ST}-b_{ST}-T.
300	\]
301	Call the resulting graph \(Q\). Assign types and labels as follows:
302	\[
303	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
304	\text{vertex}&\text{type}&\text{label}\\ \hline
305	S&0&S\\
306	a_{ST}&1&S\\
307	b_{ST}&2&T
308	\end{array}
309	\]
310	
311	Thus labels agree across edges of types \(0\!-\!1\) and \(0\!-\!2\), and are disjoint across edges of type \(1\!-\!2\).
312	
313	It follows that:
314	
315	> The endpoints of every length-\(3\) core walk having the same type have disjoint labels.
316	
317	Indeed, its type sequence goes once around \(0,1,2,0\), in one direction or the other: two label-preserving edges and one disjoint-label edge.
318	
319	The core has
320	\[
321	N=|V(F)|+2|E(F)|
322	\]
323	vertices.
324	
325	## 3.2 Three bipartite reservoirs
326	
327	Choose a positive integer \(t\). For each type \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\), add:
328	
329	* a set \(A_i=[m]\times[t]\), of size \(mt\);
330	* a set \(B_i\), of size \(kt\);
331	* all edges between \(A_i\) and \(B_i\).
332	
333	Join each core vertex of type \(i\) and label \(S\) to
334	\[
335	S\times[t]\subseteq A_i.
336	\]
337	There are no other edges. Denote this graph by \(G\).
338	
339	Its order is
340	\[
341	n=N+3(m+k)t,
342	\]
343	and every vertex has degree at least \(kt\). Thus
344	\[
345	\frac{\delta(G)}{n}
346	\ge
347	\frac{kt}{N+3(m+k)t}
348	\longrightarrow
349	\frac{k}{3(m+k)}
350	=
351	\frac{k}{9k+3(h-1)}
352	\quad(t\to\infty).
353	\tag{11}
354	\]
355	As \(k\to\infty\), the last expression tends to \(1/9\). Therefore, for any \(c<1/9\), first choose \(k\) and then \(t\) so that \(\delta(G)\ge cn\).
356	
357	## 3.3 There are no triangles or pentagons
358	
359	The core itself has no cycle shorter than \(9\).
360	
361	An odd cycle of length at most \(5\) involving a vertex of some \(B_i\) cannot lie entirely in its bipartite reservoir. Its segment through that reservoir between consecutive core vertices has length at least \(4\). A pentagon would therefore have to close with a core edge between vertices of the same type, which does not exist.
362	
363	It remains to consider cycles avoiding all \(B_i\).
364	
365	* A triangle using a reservoir vertex would require an edge between two core vertices of the same type.
366	* A pentagon using exactly one reservoir vertex would give a core path of length \(3\) between same-type vertices with intersecting labels, contrary to the displayed property of \(Q\).
367	* A pentagon using two reservoir vertices has three core vertices. Its two reservoir segments force all three core vertices to have the same type, while its remaining edge is a core edge—again impossible.
368	* Three reservoir vertices cannot occur in a \(5\)-cycle, since reservoir vertices form an independent set.
369	
370	Thus \(G\) has neither a \(C_3\) nor a \(C_5\).
371	
372	## 3.4 It cannot map to \(H\)
373	
374	Each edge \(ST\) of \(F\) is represented by a length-\(3\) path in \(G\). Under a homomorphism to a triangle-free graph, its endpoints must receive different images. Hence a homomorphism \(G\to H\) would restrict to a proper \(h\)-colouring of \(F\).
375	
376	But \(\chi(F)\ge h+1\). This is impossible.
377	
378	So every \(c<1/9\) fails, completing the lower half.

382	# 4. The Kneser fact used above
383	
384	For completeness, here is the usual short proof of the needed Kneser lower bound through the octahedral Tucker lemma.
385	
386	### Octahedral Tucker lemma
387	
388	Let
389	\[
390	\lambda:\{-1,0,1\}^m\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow
391	\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm L\}
392	\]
393	satisfy \(\lambda(-x)=-\lambda(x)\). Write \(x\preceq y\) when every nonzero coordinate of \(x\) agrees with the corresponding coordinate of \(y\).
394	
395	If
396	\[
397	x\preceq y\implies\lambda(x)\ne-\lambda(y),
398	\]
399	then \(L\ge m\).
400	
401	Here is the topological proof, including the obstruction behind the lemma. Nonzero sign vectors are the nonempty faces of the boundary of the \(m\)-dimensional cross-polytope. Chains form its barycentric subdivision. Sending the vertex \(x\) to
402	\(\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda(x))e_{|\lambda(x)|}\) and extending linearly gives an antipodal map
403	\[
404	S^{m-1}\longrightarrow S^{L-1};
405	\]
406	the no-complementary-label condition ensures that no simplex maps through \(0\).
407	
408	There is no antipodal map \(S^d\to S^{d-1}\). One standard verification uses mod-\(2\) projective cohomology: the map would descend to
409	\(\mathbb{RP}^d\to\mathbb{RP}^{d-1}\) and pull back the degree-one double-cover class \(a\) to \(a\). But \(a^d\ne0\) in \(\mathbb{RP}^d\), whereas \(a^d=0\) in \(\mathbb{RP}^{d-1}\). The first assertion can be seen directly by intersecting \(d\) generic projective hyperplanes: their intersection is one point, modulo \(2\); the second follows from dimension. Naturality gives the contradiction. The zero-dimensional cases are immediate. This proves Tucker's lemma.
410	
411	Now suppose \(KG(m,k)\) has an \(r\)-colouring. For a sign vector \(x\), put
412	\[
413	x^+=\{i:x_i=1\},\qquad x^-=\{i:x_i=-1\}.
414	\]
415	
416	* If \(|x^+|+|x^-|\le2k-2\), label \(x\) by its support size, with sign equal to its first nonzero coordinate.
417	* Otherwise, look at all \(k\)-sets contained in \(x^+\) or \(x^-\). Take the least colour occurring, and label \(x\) by \(2k-2\) plus that colour, with sign indicating the side where it occurs.
418	
419	The sign in the second rule is well-defined: the same colour cannot occur on both sides, because those two \(k\)-sets would be disjoint.
420	
421	The labelling is antipodal. Comparable vectors cannot have opposite labels. For small labels this follows because comparable vectors of the same support size are equal; for large labels, opposite labels would exhibit disjoint \(k\)-sets of the same colour. Tucker therefore gives
422	\[
423	2k-2+r\ge m,
424	\]
425	or
426	\[
427	r\ge m-2k+2,
428	\]
429	as required.

433	# 5. Python checks
434	
435	The following is executable checking code, not a program that merely prints the claimed constant. It checks:
436	
437	* the lower construction, including absence of \(C_3,C_5\), degrees and the embedded Kneser obstruction;
438	* the Kneser chromatic numbers in the tested instances, by SAT;
439	* the universal triangle-free target construction on all \(150\) nonempty \(C_3,C_5\)-free graphs in NetworkX's graph atlas;
440	* the six-disjoint-sets counting step exhaustively for reduced graphs through six vertices;
441	* the upper-bound signature construction on explicit examples;
442	* actual regularity refinements, with exact rational energy increments;
443	* exact parameter arithmetic for larger lower-bound instances.
444	
445	The mathematical arguments above establish the assertions for arbitrary sizes; finite testing is not being substituted for those arguments.
446	
447	```python
448	import itertools as it
449	import math
450	from fractions import Fraction
451	import networkx as nx
452	from z3 import Solver, Int, sat
453	
454	
455	def odd3(G):
456	    J = nx.Graph()
457	    J.add_nodes_from(G)
458	    for x in G:

272	# 3. Lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails
273	
274	We use Kneser graphs
275	\[
276	F=KG(m,k),
277	\]
278	whose vertices are the \(k\)-subsets of \([m]\), with disjoint sets adjacent. Their chromatic number is
279	\[
280	\chi(KG(m,k))=m-2k+2.
281	\tag{10}
282	\]
283	Only the lower bound in (10) is needed. A proof is included in Section 4.
284	
285	Fix a proposed triangle-free target \(H\), with \(h\) vertices. We may assume \(h\ge2\), since \(K_2\) already rules out targets with fewer vertices.
286	
287	Choose
288	\[
289	m=2k+h-1.
290	\]
291	Then \(\chi(F)\ge h+1\).
292	
293	## 3.1 The sparse core
294	
295	Orient each edge \(ST\) of \(F\) arbitrarily and replace it by
296	\[
297	S-a_{ST}-b_{ST}-T.
298	\]
299	Call the resulting graph \(Q\). Assign types and labels as follows:
300	\[
301	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
302	\text{vertex}&\text{type}&\text{label}\\ \hline
303	S&0&S\\
304	a_{ST}&1&S\\
305	b_{ST}&2&T
306	\end{array}
307	\]
308	
309	Thus labels agree across edges of types \(0\!-\!1\) and \(0\!-\!2\), and are disjoint across edges of type \(1\!-\!2\).
310	
311	It follows that:
312	
313	> The endpoints of every length-\(3\) core walk having the same type have disjoint labels.
314	
315	Indeed, its type sequence goes once around \(0,1,2,0\), in one direction or the other: two label-preserving edges and one disjoint-label edge.
316	
317	The core has
318	\[
319	N=|V(F)|+2|E(F)|
320	\]
321	vertices.
322	
323	## 3.2 Three bipartite reservoirs
324	
325	Choose a positive integer \(t\). For each type \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\), add:
326	
327	* a set \(A_i=[m]\times[t]\), of size \(mt\);
328	* a set \(B_i\), of size \(kt\);
329	* all edges between \(A_i\) and \(B_i\).
330	
331	Join each core vertex of type \(i\) and label \(S\) to
332	\[
333	S\times[t]\subseteq A_i.
334	\]
335	There are no other edges. Denote this graph by \(G\).
336	
337	Its order is
338	\[
339	n=N+3(m+k)t,
340	\]
341	and every vertex has degree at least \(kt\). Thus
342	\[
343	\frac{\delta(G)}{n}
344	\ge
345	\frac{kt}{N+3(m+k)t}
346	\longrightarrow
347	\frac{k}{3(m+k)}
348	=
349	\frac{k}{9k+3(h-1)}
350	\quad(t\to\infty).
351	\tag{11}
352	\]
353	As \(k\to\infty\), the last expression tends to \(1/9\). Therefore, for any \(c<1/9\), first choose \(k\) and then \(t\) so that \(\delta(G)\ge cn\).
354	
355	## 3.3 There are no triangles or pentagons
356	
357	The core itself has no cycle shorter than \(9\).
358	
359	An odd cycle of length at most \(5\) involving a vertex of some \(B_i\) cannot lie entirely in its bipartite reservoir. Its segment through that reservoir between consecutive core vertices has length at least \(4\). A pentagon would therefore have to close with a core edge between vertices of the same type, which does not exist.
360	
361	It remains to consider cycles avoiding all \(B_i\).
362	
363	* A triangle using a reservoir vertex would require an edge between two core vertices of the same type.
364	* A pentagon using exactly one reservoir vertex would give a core path of length \(3\) between same-type vertices with intersecting labels, contrary to the displayed property of \(Q\).
365	* A pentagon using two reservoir vertices has three core vertices. Its two reservoir segments force all three core vertices to have the same type, while its remaining edge is a core edge—again impossible.
366	* Three reservoir vertices cannot occur in a \(5\)-cycle, since reservoir vertices form an independent set.
367	
368	Thus \(G\) has neither a \(C_3\) nor a \(C_5\).
369	
370	## 3.4 It cannot map to \(H\)
371	
372	Each edge \(ST\) of \(F\) is represented by a length-\(3\) path in \(G\). Under a homomorphism to a triangle-free graph, its endpoints must receive different images. Hence a homomorphism \(G\to H\) would restrict to a proper \(h\)-colouring of \(F\).
373	
374	But \(\chi(F)\ge h+1\). This is impossible.
375	
376	So every \(c<1/9\) fails, completing the lower half.

380	# 4. The Kneser fact used above
381	
382	For completeness, here is the usual short proof of the needed Kneser lower bound through the octahedral Tucker lemma.
383	
384	### Octahedral Tucker lemma
385	
386	Let
387	\[
388	\lambda:\{-1,0,1\}^m\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow
389	\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm L\}
390	\]
391	satisfy \(\lambda(-x)=-\lambda(x)\). Write \(x\preceq y\) when every nonzero coordinate of \(x\) agrees with the corresponding coordinate of \(y\).
392	
393	If
394	\[
395	x\preceq y\implies\lambda(x)\ne-\lambda(y),
396	\]
397	then \(L\ge m\).
398	
399	Here is the topological proof, including the obstruction behind the lemma. Nonzero sign vectors are the nonempty faces of the boundary of the \(m\)-dimensional cross-polytope. Chains form its barycentric subdivision. Sending the vertex \(x\) to
400	\(\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda(x))e_{|\lambda(x)|}\) and extending linearly gives an antipodal map
401	\[
402	S^{m-1}\longrightarrow S^{L-1};
403	\]
404	the no-complementary-label condition ensures that no simplex maps through \(0\).
405	
406	There is no antipodal map \(S^d\to S^{d-1}\). One standard verification uses mod-\(2\) projective cohomology: the map would descend to
407	\(\mathbb{RP}^d\to\mathbb{RP}^{d-1}\) and pull back the degree-one double-cover class \(a\) to \(a\). But \(a^d\ne0\) in \(\mathbb{RP}^d\), whereas \(a^d=0\) in \(\mathbb{RP}^{d-1}\). The first assertion can be seen directly by intersecting \(d\) generic projective hyperplanes: their intersection is one point, modulo \(2\); the second follows from dimension. Naturality gives the contradiction. The zero-dimensional cases are immediate. This proves Tucker's lemma.
408	
409	Now suppose \(KG(m,k)\) has an \(r\)-colouring. For a sign vector \(x\), put
410	\[
411	x^+=\{i:x_i=1\},\qquad x^-=\{i:x_i=-1\}.
412	\]
413	
414	* If \(|x^+|+|x^-|\le2k-2\), label \(x\) by its support size, with sign equal to its first nonzero coordinate.
415	* Otherwise, look at all \(k\)-sets contained in \(x^+\) or \(x^-\). Take the least colour occurring, and label \(x\) by \(2k-2\) plus that colour, with sign indicating the side where it occurs.
416	
417	The sign in the second rule is well-defined: the same colour cannot occur on both sides, because those two \(k\)-sets would be disjoint.
418	
419	The labelling is antipodal. Comparable vectors cannot have opposite labels. For small labels this follows because comparable vectors of the same support size are equal; for large labels, opposite labels would exhibit disjoint \(k\)-sets of the same colour. Tucker therefore gives
420	\[
421	2k-2+r\ge m,
422	\]
423	or
424	\[
425	r\ge m-2k+2,
426	\]
427	as required.
